messages.author: a8d314c9e9addfaa
messages.subject: Area covered and replicates
parts:
Hi I am just a beginner in Distance and I would like to know if someone can explain me few things about the Software.
1)Maybe I found something in the distance help, but I am not sure, so I ask:how do I take account of the various replicates when I do the input of data?
2)I have done a transect survey, but we were in a forest and it wasn't possible to have straight transects, so for this survey the area can't be calculated as A=2wl, because for some transects many portions of the area covered overlap and so this area is inferior to the value that would be obtained with the formula.I have calculated the area covered for each trasect, but is there a way of putting this information in the software?
Thanks

Dayrone

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Area covered and replicates
parts:
Dayrone

Welcome to the list.  It is not obvious from your question whether you are using the stand-alone Distance for Windows software http://distancesampling.org/Distance/index.html , or the package called Distance that is run using R.  I speculate that you are using R, because Distance for Windows provides guidance on structuring data for input.  If I'm wrong, please write again and correct me.

By "replicates" I assume you mean transects.  We have several data sets online that you can examine to see how they are structured.  For example,
  • http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/ducknests.csv consists of data from 20 transects, all of the same length, within a single stratum
  • http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.csv contains data from 25 transects; 13 in stratum "South" and 12 in stratum "North".  In this dataset, there are a number of transects on which no detections were made.  Note how these are recorded.
For your second question regarding area.  The software does not need the value of a=2lw to perform its calculations.  The overlap between transects is not of great concern.  Consider an extreme case of overlap: each transect is walked twice.  That results in complete overlap of transects.  This is a common type of survey design, for example, when transects need to be cut. This poses no problem in analysis, as long as the effort associated with transects reflects the length is double the physical length of the transect.

I hope this is helpful.

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Area covered and replicates
parts:
Dayrone

Before you import your data into Distance for Windows, multiply each of your transect lengths by the number of times you walked the transects.  That will ensure that you have effort correctly computed and also produces the correct number of physical transects in your study.
